stem:
A 23-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by paramedics following a motor vehicle collision.  He was an unrestrained passenger in the front seat.  Several days after hospitalization, his fluid volume and serum osmolarity are depicted in the image below (solid line = normal; dotted line = patient).  The y-axis shows osmolarity and the x-axis shows compartment fluid volumes.

Which of the following conditions is the most likely cause of the findings shown in the image?​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​
explanation:
This patient's extracellular fluid (ECF) and intracellular fluid (ICF) compartment volumes are decreased, alongside increased osmolarity.  This pattern is consistent with hyperosmotic volume contraction, caused by loss of electrolyte-free water.  Water loss begins in the ECF (from renally filtered plasma), decreasing ECF volume and increasing its osmolarity.  Elevated ECF osmolarity subsequently draws water from the ICF until osmolarities are equal (but higher than baseline).

Free water loss may stem from nonrenal causes (eg, water deprivation, excessive sweating) or renal mechanisms.  Excessive renal water excretion occurs due to impaired secretion or action of arginine vasopressin (AVP) [ie, antidiuretic hormone (ADH)].  Causes include AVP resistance or deficiency, formerly known as nephrogenic and central diabetes insipidus, respectively.  AVP deficiency frequently occurs following severe motor vehicle collisions (eg, unrestrained passengers) due to blunt head trauma that disrupts AVP (ADH) secretion.

Elevated osmolarity rapidly triggers thirst, and increased water consumption typically normalizes ECF/ICF volumes and osmolarity.  However, hospitalized patients who are unable to drink may develop hyperosmotic volume contraction (as in this patient).  Treatment involves AVP analogues such as desmopressin (in AVP deficiency) to prevent further water loss.  In addition, exogenous free water administration (eg, IV dextrose with water) may be required to replace free water losses.

(Choice A)  Acute gastrointestinal hemorrhage (or diarrhea) causes loss of fluid from the ECF that has the same osmolarity (isosmotic) as the rest of the ECF (ie, isosmotic volume contraction).  ICF volume and osmolarity are unaffected because there is no osmotic gradient to shift water between compartments.

(Choice C)  Hypertonic saline contains a higher sodium concentration than plasma, leading to an increase in ECF osmolarity following infusion.  The added fluid volume also increases the ECF.  Elevated ECF osmolarity pulls water from the ICF, decreasing ICF volume and further increasing ECF volume.  The net result is increased osmolarity of both compartments, with expansion of the ECF volume and decreased ICF volume (ie, hyperosmotic volume expansion).

(Choice D)  Primary adrenal insufficiency is characterized by a deficiency in aldosterone and cortisol (due to adrenal failure).  Aldosterone loss causes urinary sodium excretion, which reduces ECF volume and causes hypotension.  Concurrent cortisol deficiency exacerbates hypotension (by impairing vascular tone).  Hypotension triggers ADH release (volume stimulus), promoting water retention with decreased ECF osmolarity.  Low ECF osmolarity shifts fluid into the ICF, increasing ICF volume (although combined volume is reduced).  This shift leads to the ICF osmolarity decreasing until it matches ECF osmolarity.  The net result is hyposmotic volume contraction (ECF loss exceeds ICF gain).

(Choice E)  Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion leads to excess free water retention, resulting in effects that are directly opposite those of AVP deficiency/resistance.  Water is first retained in the ECF (into the plasma), increasing ECF volume and lowering its osmolarity.  Reduced ECF osmolarity drives water into the ICF until osmolarities are equal (but lower than baseline).  The net result is decreased osmolarity and increased volumes of both compartments (ie, hyposmotic volume expansion).  Over time, compensatory mechanisms—including suppression of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and secretion of natriuretic peptides—promote sodium excretion, restoring euvolemia.  However, inappropriate ADH secretion maintains a hyposmotic state (ie, euvolemic hyponatremia).

Educational objective:Hyperosmotic volume contraction is caused by the loss of electrolyte-free water, which results in decreased extracellular fluid (ECF) and intracellular fluid (ICF) volumes.  Because of the loss of free water, osmolarity is increased in both the ECF and ICF.  Clinically, this is seen in patients with excess renal water excretion due to arginine vasopressin deficiency or resistance (formerly diabetes insipidus).​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​
